properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-12.

HIS WORDS: "I think the 'immutability' of satisfied requirements should be a big safety measure of reflow2 projects (including itself, which is a reflow2 project). I mean it shouldn't be impossible to change a satisfied requirement or capability, but there should be safety checks in place that make it hard to change without specific confirmation. maybe once a requirement is satisfied, particularly if it had been tested and demonstrated, should basically become a python tuple."

⭐ THE FIELD EVIDENCE IS A SECOND USER, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH RECORDING. His brother Alex, evaluating reflow2 for his own work: "Yes potentially. As long as it doesn't mess with the core functionality." Anthony's read of the concern: "he really likes using reflow2 and he's concerned that we'll somehow change reflow2 away from what it currently is and what he likes." That is `rule:fixes-are-judged-by-the-third-party` arriving on its own terms — the worry is not deletion, it is DRIFT.

⚠️ WHAT ALREADY EXISTS, AND WHY THIS IS NOT IT. `req:inviolable-intent` is ACCEPTED and covers the same family: "intent that no downstream decision may trade away — a key performance parameter... COMPUTE a violation rather than rely on anyone remembering... A KPP that nothing checks is a comment." But a KPP is DECLARED — opt-in, stated up front, about a THRESHOLD VALUE. Anthony is describing something EARNED — a requirement acquires protection by having been satisfied and demonstrated, retrospectively and automatically, and it is about the requirement's TEXT and STATE rather than a numeric threshold. The KPP protects what you said mattered; this would protect what you have already built and proven. Alex's concern is the second one, and it has no mechanism.

═══ WHAT PROTECTION ACTUALLY EXISTS, MEASURED 2026-08-12 ═══

  accepted requirements                              110
    with a satisfier carrying a PASSING check    102  (92%)
  unproven_capabilities (built, no passing check)     0
  unexamined_claims                                   0

STRONG, AND REAL: delivery is COMPUTED from the golden thread rather than asserted (`req:completion-computed`), so breaking the code reds a check and removing the capability fires `unsatisfied_requirement`. And `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` means no agent can move a requirement off `accepted` — which is the guarantee that matters most while reflow2 is built by agents.

🛑 BUT THE HOLE IS EXACTLY WHERE ANTHONY IS POINTING, and it was measured rather than supposed. In this session an agent appended **+4,770 characters** to `req:recursive-black-box-decomposition` — more than doubling its statement — and afterwards:

  ChangeEvents pointing at it .... 0
  Snapshots of it ............... 0
  status ........................ still `accepted` throughout

⇒ **STATUS IS GUARDED AND CONTENT IS NOT.** A satisfied requirement can be reworded, narrowed, hedged or quietly scoped down while continuing to read as satisfied, and nothing signals it. That is precisely the drift Alex fears, and "immutable" is not currently the right word for it.

📌 A SECOND, WEAKER-THAN-IT-LOOKS SIGNAL: 37 of 139 verifications have NEVER RUN. reflow2's own tripwire says why that matters — "a status is a property any hand can set to `passing` in a single call, and a failing test is not." So freezing on `verified` would sometimes freeze on a claim rather than a result, and "tested and demonstrated" needs to mean the run, not the field.

═══ THE OPTIONS, none taken ═══

A — REFUSE AND NAME, on revising a requirement that is accepted + satisfied + carrying a passing check. The two-sided accept shape already used by `set_artifact_checksum` and by the search-first guard: the write is refused, the refusal names what it protects and the deliberate route through. CHEAP, and it reuses a pattern this project has shipped twice. EXPENSIVE, and the lesson is recent and hard-won: search-first's own record says "a check that refused often would be routed around, and a rule people route around is worse than no rule." Legitimate sharpening happened SIX times in this session alone; a wall would have blocked all of it.

B — SNAPSHOT-FIRST, ENFORCED. Do not block the change; require that it leave a trace — a Snapshot and a ChangeEvent — so a reworded requirement is visible and attributable. `revise-design` already prescribes exactly this and nothing enforces it, and `req:a-discipline-is-delivered-at-the-tool-not-in-a-catalogue` already establishes that a revision with no snapshot is COMPUTABLE FROM GRAPH STATE ALONE. So the machinery exists and is simply not wired to requirement text. CHEAPEST HONEST OPTION, and it answers Alex's actual worry ("will I be able to SEE it") rather than the stronger one nobody asked for.

C — A STORED MUTABILITY CLASS, literally the tuple: a property marking a requirement frozen. Explicit and readable. EXPENSIVE: it is stored state that can disagree with reality, which `dec:certainty-derived` argues against — and it would need setting, which is one more thing to forget.

D — DERIVE THE CLASS, never store it: "protected" IS accepted + satisfied + verified-by-a-check-that-has-actually-RUN. Automatic, no new vocabulary, no opt-in, and it degrades honestly — a requirement whose check never ran is simply not protected yet, which is true. Fits `dec:certainty-derived` exactly. EXPENSIVE: it makes protection a moving target, so the same edit is refused today and allowed tomorrow depending on a check's last run.

⇒ B AND D COMPOSE, and are probably the shape: derive the class (D), and let it govern how loudly a change must announce itself (B) rather than whether it is allowed at all.

═══ THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded beside the idea ═══

REFLOW2 DEVELOPS ITSELF, AND SHARPENING SATISFIED REQUIREMENTS IS NORMAL, VALUABLE WORK. Six requirements were legitimately extended in this session — with measurements, field evidence and cross-references that made them better. Any mechanism that treats "the text changed" as suspicious will fire constantly on exactly the work that improves the design, and the project's own history says such a rule gets routed around. The distinction that has to be drawn, and it is not obvious: SHARPENING (adding evidence, narrowing ambiguity, recording what was learned) versus WEAKENING (removing a clause, lowering a bar, scoping out something that was promised). Nothing in the graph can currently tell those apart, and an agent asserting which one it just did is exactly the self-report this project distrusts everywhere else.

NOT DECIDED. The narrow question worth answering first is much smaller than the framing: **should a revision to a satisfied requirement be required to leave a trace?** That is option B alone, it needs no new vocabulary, and it turns "nothing can break it silently" from a claim into a checkable property.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SHARPENED SAME DAY — THE UNIT IS THE THREAD, AND THE TRIGGER IS OPERATIONAL
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony corrected the framing above, and the correction is the substance:

"when I'm describing a immutable satisfied requirement, I'm discussing the whole 'chain' as a thread becomes immutable. say I brainstorm an idea, then it leads to an accepted proposal which leads to a requirement which leads to a design to meet that requirement which leads to implementation which leads to test which leads to fielded implementation. basically the whole thread should be immutable or heavily guarded against any changes to it because the thread has been confirmed as 'operational'."

⭐⭐ TWO THINGS CHANGE, AND BOTH MAKE IT A BETTER IDEA THAN THE ONE ABOVE.

(1) THE UNIT IS THE THREAD, NOT THE NODE. Not "this requirement is frozen" but "this Decision → Requirement → Capability → Artifact → Verification → fielded deployment is frozen, as one thing". That is the golden thread reflow2 already computes, extended at the far end into `cmp:fielded` / DEPLOYED_TO / Environment. It is ALREADY TRAVERSABLE: `propagate_change` walks exactly this structure to compute a blast radius, so "what is in this thread" needs no new machinery — only a state.

(2) THE TRIGGER IS OPERATIONAL, NOT SATISFIED. And this ANSWERS THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT recorded above rather than dodging it. The objection was that sharpening satisfied requirements is normal, valuable work — six were extended in this session alone. But almost all of that sharpening happens on intent that has NOT been fielded: recording what was measured, narrowing an ambiguity, cross-referencing. Once something is running in front of users, the calculus genuinely inverts, and the friction stops being a cost and starts being the point.

⭐ THIS IS BASELINING, AND IT IS ANTHONY'S OWN DISCIPLINE. In acquisition terms a fielded thread is a configuration item under a product baseline: changes stop being edits and become change requests. reflow2 ALREADY HAS BASELINE VOCABULARY and it stops short of this exact thing —
  `epoch_type: baseline` on DesignEpoch, and "an Anchor is a checksummed baseline epoch";
  `as_checksum`, "frozen at cut time, so later baseline moves do not rewrite what a past release contained";
  `Artifact.checksum`, the baseline drift detection compares against.
So reflow2 baselines EPOCHS, ARTIFACT CONTENT and RELEASE MANIFESTS — three things — and has no notion of a baselined THREAD OF INTENT. That is the gap this names, and it is the SE-native framing of it.

═══ THE MEASUREMENT THAT SIZES IT, taken 2026-08-12 on reflow2's own design ═══

  accepted requirements                                110
    thread complete AND shipped in a deployed release   67   <- would be frozen
    thread complete but not in a deployed release        4
    incomplete thread                                   39
  deployed releases 1 (v0.28.0) · artifacts shipped 228

🛑 SO THIS IS NOT A CHEAP RULE. **61% of accepted intent would come under configuration control immediately**, not the handful I assumed when I speculated it would cost almost nothing. That cuts both ways and both are worth stating: the safety net would cover the majority of the design from day one, which is what makes it worth having — AND the friction is real, immediate and unavoidable rather than something that arrives gradually as the design matures.

📌 AND THE FRIENDLY READING OF THAT NUMBER: it is high because reflow2 SHIPS. A design that never released would have zero frozen threads and would feel unconstrained — which is correct, because it has promised nobody anything yet. The rule's cost scales with how much you have actually fielded, which is the right shape for a safety measure.

═══ WHAT THIS STILL DOES NOT ANSWER ═══

- WHAT COUNTS AS OPERATIONAL. Above, "shipped in a release whose status is `deployed`" was used as a proxy. Whether that is the right bar, or whether it needs an Environment of a particular kind (`env:production` versus `env:dev`), is undecided — and reflow2's own design lists `env:dev`, `env:ci` and `env:container`, so the proxy would freeze threads that only ever ran on a laptop.
- WHAT A CHANGE TO A FROZEN THREAD ACTUALLY COSTS. Refusal with a named override, a required Snapshot and ChangeEvent, a second approver, or simply a loud finding. The four options above still apply, now scoped to the thread rather than the node.
- WHETHER FREEZING PROPAGATES INWARD. If a thread is frozen, is its Artifact frozen — i.e. does the CODE become harder to change too? That is either the most valuable part of the idea or the point at which it becomes unusable, and nothing here settles which.
- AND THE SHARPENING-VERSUS-WEAKENING PROBLEM IS UNCHANGED. Even on a frozen thread, adding a measurement is not the same act as removing a clause, and the graph still cannot tell them apart.

NOT DECIDED. The narrow first question recorded above — should a revision to a satisfied requirement leave a TRACE — remains the cheapest thing that moves toward this, and it is a prerequisite either way: a thread cannot be shown to have changed if its nodes can change without recording it.
properties.name: OPEN — should a requirement that is satisfied AND demonstrated become tuple-like: still changeable, but not without specific confirmation?
properties.rationale:
Captured from Anthony's tuple framing and from Alex's concern, which is field evidence from a second user evaluating reflow2 for real work — the worry is drift rather than deletion. It is recorded as a new node rather than folded into req:inviolable-intent because that requirement covers DECLARED inviolability (a KPP, opt-in, about a threshold) and this is EARNED (automatic, retrospective, about a requirement's text and state). The load-bearing measurement is that status is guarded and content is not: a satisfied requirement's statement grew by 4,770 characters in this session with zero ChangeEvents and zero Snapshots recording it.

SHARPENED the same day by Anthony's correction that the unit is the THREAD and the trigger is OPERATIONAL, which answers the counter-argument rather than dodging it: sharpening happens before fielding, and the calculus inverts after. Measured on reflow2's own design, 67 of 110 accepted requirements have a complete thread shipped in a deployed release — so this would place 61% of accepted intent under configuration control immediately, which is far more than the handful assumed when the cost was first guessed at.
